articles.title: Is it a missile? Is it a drone? What’s the Pelican used by Ukraine?
articles.body:
Is it a missile? Is it a drone? What’s the Pelican used by Ukraine?
The use of the Pelican has sparked interest among military analysts about whether it was a tactical ballistic missile or a drone.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday’s large-scale strike on Russia involved several weapons, including a “Pelican” for the first time.
In a post on X on Sunday morning, Zelenskyy wrote that long-range attacks on Moscow’s region had a “very significant impact”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions over Ukraine war
- list 2 of 3Could US pull one-third of troops from Europe? What that would mean
- list 3 of 3Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
“One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine. The systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen and Pelican,” he said.
The attack on the final day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary elections killed at least three people. Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said more than 1,600 drones were intercepted, 450 of them heading for the capital.
However, the use of the Pelican has interested military analysts about whether it is a tactical ballistic missile or a drone.
Here’s what we know:
What is a Pelican missile and why is there confusion?
Speaking at the 34th International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland last week, the CEO of Ukrainian defence firm Fire Point said Ukraine could start deploying its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile to target Russia in weeks, reported The Kyiv Post.
Iryna Terekh explained that the new weapons could strike targets 200km (125 miles) away and carry a warhead weighing up to 150kg.
The FP-7 system is ground-launched and has a maximum projectile speed of 1,500 metres per second. Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman told Ukrainian media back in March that the system is cheaper than the US-made Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) surface-to-surface ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy also said last month that they expected to use their first domestically produced ballistic missile as early as in the autumn.
So far, there is no official confirmation that the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile is the Pelican, but Ukrainian media, such as The Kyiv Post, has linked the two together.
The New Voice of Ukraine reported on Sunday that Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that also produces the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile, had earlier this year applied to register the Pelican trademark.
However, the RBC-Ukraine news agency, citing unnamed sources, reported on Sunday without elaborating that the Pelican was an aircraft-type drone.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the Ukrainian media reports.
What is Ukraine’s weapons production like?
In February, Ukraine’s defence ministry said that the domestic weapons industry had demonstrated “unprecedented growth”, with production capacity increasing 50-fold to $50bn.
“As a result, domestic manufacturers now meet over half of the Defence Forces’ needs for weapons and military equipment,” the ministry said.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy posted on X that the military counterintelligence unit at the Security Service of Ukraine has developed a new interceptor drone that had been “successfully deployed” against Iranian-made Shahed drones used by Russia throughout the war to target Ukraine.
“Step by step, we are moving forward to give Ukraine greater protection. I thank all the developers and manufacturers who work every day to scale up the weapons we need,” he said.
In March, Oleksandr Syrskyi, the former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, said more than 70 per cent of Shahed-type attack drones were destroyed using interceptor drones in February.
The success of Ukraine’s drone interceptors also led to interest from Gulf states targeted by Iranian drones and missiles during the US-Israeli war.
How have attacks on Russia changed recently?
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified attacks on each other’s infrastructure, targeting oil facilities and logistics hubs.
Ukraine has also repeatedly struck warehouses belonging to Russia’s Wildberries e-commerce giant since July, in what has been described as an attack on Moscow’s supply chains and to hurt the Russian economy.
On Monday, the Financial Times reported that US President Donald Trump spoke to Zelenskyy on Sunday, urging him to stop attacking Russian refineries over concerns that it was worsening the global shortage of diesel and causing fuel prices to increase.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade blows ahead of Zelenskyy meeting with Trump
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed at least four people overnight, officials said Tuesday, while a Ukrainian long-range strike damaged another Russian oil refinery.
The ongoing exchange of daily aerial attacks, while positions on the battlefield's front line barely change, provided a backdrop to the visit by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the United States.
Zelenskyy was due to meet other world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader is hoping to recruit their help to end Russia's more than 41/2-year-old full-scale invasion of his country.
Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't due to attend the annual event.
The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions.
The repeated attacks on Russian refineries, following Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's power grid, have caused international shortages of diesel and price spikes, according to Trump. However, the global crunch also came after the Iran war led to curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that his country would provide Ukraine with more radars to help protect its power grid.
He said on social media that he discussed with Trump the possibility of a truce between Moscow and Kyiv on strikes on energy infrastructure and a "moratorium" on Black Sea attacks.
Zelenskyy began his New York visit by meeting with U.S. senators, thanking them for what he called strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for recently passing a tougher Russian sanctions bill that Trump has signed into law.
Peace and security will be closer once the bill is fully implemented, he said.
Zelenskyy said on social media that he briefed senators on his proposals for de-escalation measures that he intends to discuss with Trump later Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader also plans to again press Trump to send more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Kyiv desperately needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles.
Ukraine said that it struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, in an overnight attack.
Several drones hit their targets, sparking a large fire at the facility, according to a statement from Ukrainian special forces.
The refinery, owned by Rosneft, is a key fuel supplier for central Russia, producing gasoline, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products, the statement said. Ukraine said that it struck the same refinery last June.
One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones.
The Russian Defense Ministry Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula.
Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said.
The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration.
The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine.
They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.

articles.title: ‘Incurable headache’ to enemies: North Korea tests new weapon system (PHOTOS)
articles.body:
‘Incurable headache’ to enemies: North Korea tests new weapon system (PHOTOS)
North Korea’s missile agency has tested a “new-type weapon,” according to Pyongyang’s state media. Seoul said two short-range ballistic missiles were fired on Sunday toward the Sea of Japan.
North Korean reports did not specify what was new about the unit, saying only that the test was “of great significance” to the nation’s military. State media released several photos showing the launch of a road-mobile missile tipped with what appeared to be a hypersonic glide vehicle.
Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un oversaw the test and said that his country’s possession of “ultra-modern defense technology” serves as a deterrent and would “give the enemy an incurable headache.”
Senior officials from South Korea, Japan and the US held phone consultations on Monday to discuss their response to the test, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said.
Local media linked the launch to the multinational Pacific Vanguard maritime exercise held in August and September. Warships from Australia, Canada, Japan, South Korea and the US participated in the drills. Pyongyang views US-led military exercises in the region as a threat to its national security and has frequently responded with demonstrations of military force.
In recent years, Kim’s government has abandoned Korean unification as an overarching policy goal and formally designated South Korea as a separate hostile state. The shift has not been fully mirrored in Seoul, although the government of South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has made some adjustments to its messaging in that direction.
Lee’s Democratic Party of Korea generally favors reducing tensions with Pyongyang, in contrast with the conservative People Power Party. In an interview with The New York Times last week, Lee suggested that some relief from international sanctions on North Korea could encourage it to slow its weapons development.
“I believe there is significant value in a trade-off between sanctions – which are not particularly effective anyway – and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology,” he said.
“Aiming for denuclearization under the current circumstances,” Lee added, “guarantees that nothing will be accomplished.”
US President Donald Trump has recently taken a more conciliatory tone toward North Korea. In August, he suggested that an in-person meeting with Kim could be arranged after the Pentagon cut short a joint military exercise with Seoul.
The Trump administration’s international standing has suffered a number of blows recently, primarily due to his decision to launch a war with Iran, which has significantly disrupted the global energy market.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Military-industrial, energy, metallurgy facilities hit in strike by Russian army
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s metallurgical, chemical, military-industrial, and fuel and energy facilities in Kiev, and in the Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, and Odesa Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has summarized the main information on the results of the strikes.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- The Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike using precision land-, sea-, and air-based weapons, as well as unmanned aerial vehicles, against targets in Ukraine overnight, the ministry reported.
- The strikes targeted facilities in the metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as Ukrainian port infrastructure in Kiev and the Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, and Odessa Regions, and naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian armed forces, it stated.
- During the massive nighttime strike, Russian troops used sea-launched Tsirkon hypersonic missiles, the ministry reported on its Max channel.
Targets destroyed
- According to the ministry, an industrial facility in Kiev (Fire Point LLC), which manufactured components and warheads for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, and a fuel and lubricants warehouse (Grandterminal LLC), used by the Ukrainian armed forces as a logistics hub for receiving and distributing diesel fuel, were struck in Kiev.
- Also, in Kremenchug, Poltava Region, the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory was struck. Its production facilities were being used to manufacture small-arms ammunition for the needs of the Ukrainian armed forces.
- In addition, Russian forces hit a steel mill in Krivoy Rog, Dnepropetrovsk Region, which produced steel products for military manufacturing.
- A pipe rolling mill (Interpipe Steel) in Dnepropetrovsk that manufactured and supplied rolled metal products for the production of components (fuselages, power units, wings, and other elements) for long-range UAVs was also struck.
- In addition, three Sirius Extrusion logistics centers in Dnepropetrovsk that stored and distributed cargo intended to supply the Ukrainian armed forces, were struck.
- A facility producing solid rocket propellant and gunpowder (Sovrakhim) was struck in Pavlograd, Dnepropetrovsk Region. It manufactured warheads and rocket propellant components for Fire Point’s FP-9 ballistic missiles.
- In addition, a railway infrastructure facility in Vinnitsa was struck.
- Russian forces hit two logistics centers in Odessa and a Nova Post logistics center in Ilyichevsk, Odessa Region, which were used to store and distribute military and dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- Furthermore, a dry cargo ship delivering military cargo to the Odessa port was struck at sea.
- Port infrastructure facilities used for unloading and storing military cargo and fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian army were struck at the Reni port in the Odessa Region.
Situation in Ukraine
- Ukrainian media reported explosions in Kiev, Dnepropetrovsk, Kropivnitsky, Krivoy Rog, and Chernigov overnight and on Tuesday morning.
- A fire broke out at warehouses in Kiev, the city’s military administration reported.
- According to information published on its Telegram channel, the warehouse facilities are located in the Goloseyevsky district of the city.
- A production facility, warehouses, and a factory were damaged as a result of explosions in the Kiev Region, said Timur Tkachenko, the head of the regional administration.
- According to information published on his Telegram channel, warehouses, production facilities, and an enterprise located in the Bucha, Obukhov, Brovary, and Belaya Tserkov districts of the Kiev Region, were hit.
- Industrial facilities in Dnepropetrovsk, Krivoy Rog, and Pavlograd in the Dnepropetrovsk Region in southeastern Ukraine were damaged and caught fire as a result of the strikes, the head of the regional administration, Alexander Ganza, reported.
- About 100,000 customers were left without electricity in the Chernigov Region in northern Ukraine as a power facility was damaged in the neighboring region, the Chernigovoblenergo regional power distribution company reported.
- According to the company’s Telegram channel, customers in four districts of the region--Koryukovsky, Novgorod-Seversky, Nezhinsky, and Chernigovsky--were left without power.
- The location of the damaged power facility was not specified.
- A critical infrastructure facility was damaged in the Poltava Region in northeastern Ukraine, according to the regional administration head Vitaly Dyakovnich.
- The facility is located in the Kremenchug district, he reported on Telegram.
- A local industrial enterprise was also damaged.
- Odessa in southern Ukraine is covered in black smoke due to a fire on the outskirts of the city. The authorities are conducting air quality measurements, Sergey Lysak, the head of the city’s military administration, said.
- Nova Post warehouses are burning on the outskirts of Odessa, the Ukrainian online publication Strana reported.

articles.title: North Korea reports new missile test designed to give enemy 'incurable headache'
articles.body:
North Korea said it successfully tested a new weapon showcasing "ultra-modern defense technology" on Sunday, in a launch overseen by leader Kim Jong Un, who praised progress in strengthening the country's war readiness, state media reported on Tuesday.
Kim said the test, conducted by North Korea's Missile Administration, demonstrated a significant development in the country's armed forces' ability to fight, and "the enemy will know better what such progress means without any explanation."
"He affirmed that such reality would give the enemy an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow," Kim was cited as saying.
The KCNA report did not specify the type of weapon tested.
Photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, accompanied by his teenage daughter, inspecting a screen displaying a map of the country's east coast and the "flight trajectory" of Hwasongpho-11-ma-1, likely part of a series of short-range ballistic missiles Pyongyang is upgrading.
North Korea fires ballistic missile into ocean
NK News, a Seoul-based website specializing in North Korea, said the projectile appeared to be an upgraded variant of a missile equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle.
Mounting a glide vehicle on a missile means the warhead can maneuver to evade anti-missile defenses and also potentially be launched partially into orbit.
Hypersonic missiles are among a range of weapons that Kim has called for development to upgrade its nuclear capabilities.
The South Korean military said on Sunday that North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast.
The test came days after Pyongyang accused the US of raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills.
On Monday, the foreign ministers of South Korea, Japan, and the United States met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to agree to coordinate closely on peace, stability, and denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula, according to Seoul's foreign ministry.

articles.title: What F-16 Gun Kills Tell Us About the Future of Ukraine’s Air Force
articles.body:
A remarkable cockpit photograph released by Ukraine last week captures far more than the destruction of a Russian Geran jet-powered attack drone. It illustrates both how far the Ukrainian Air Force has come—and the gap between the force it has today and the one it would need to become a major European air power in the future.
This is important because the future of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself does not depend on getting a few more F-16s, but rather on its ability to build an air force capable of the challenge.
The photograph is extraordinary. Taken from the cockpit of a Ukrainian F-16 during a Russian mass air attack on Sept. 10 and released a week later, the image shows a Geran drone falling from the sky, trailing smoke. According to my sources in Ukraine, it was the pilot’s third gun kill of the sortie.
Think about that for a moment.
An aircraft designed during the Cold War and transferred to Ukraine after decades of service in Western Europe, is being flown by a pilot with the Ukrainian Air Force against Russian cruise missiles in an air war unlike anything NATO has previously experienced. And the pilot is shooting them down with the F-16’s 20mm cannon.
On the night of Sept. 9-10, Russia launched 149 Shahed-type cruise missiles, along with decoys and other unmanned aircraft, against Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, 128 were destroyed or suppressed. Roughly half of these were Gerans, which are jet-powered variants of the Shahed.
The photograph is not only a terrific advertisement for the ingenuity and skill of airmen in Ukraine, but also a warning to those drawing the wrong conclusions about airpower from this conflict.
Ukraine’s success with the F-16 does not mean these aircraft are sufficient for its long-term needs.
The F-16 Ukraine Has Is Not the F-16 of Today
The European aircraft originally provided to Ukraine are principally F-16AM/BM Mid-Life Update aircraft. They began life as older Block 15 F-16 fighters and subsequently received substantial avionics and weapons upgrades. They remain capable airplanes, and they have been modernized with capabilities comparable to later F-16C/D models. But there is an important distinction between an upgraded aircraft conceived more than 40 years ago and what the F-16 has become today.
The newest F-16 Block 70/72 aircraft are equipped with the APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, enhanced mission computers and electronic warfare capabilities, advanced datalinks, updated cockpit displays, infrared search-and-track integration, and compatibility with a wide range of modern weapons. Its upgraded airframe is rated for a 12,000-hour structural service life.
The APG-83 is derived from the AESA radars used in the F-22 and F-35, providing pilots greater situational awareness, electronic protection, and the ability to search and track targets more effectively in a complex electromagnetic environment. That matters enormously over Ukraine.
The Ukrainian Air Force is not confronting a single threat. Its pilots face an extraordinarily complicated mixture of slow propeller-driven drones, faster jet-powered Gerans, cruise missiles, Russian fighters, long-range surface-to-air missile systems, electronic warfare, and dense ground-based air defenses.
A modern fighter must therefore do much more than fly fast and carry missiles. It needs to find, identify, prioritize, share, and engage multiple threats while surviving in a heavily contested electromagnetic environment. That is fundamentally an information problem—and modern sensors, electronic warfare and networking are what increasingly determine success.
Shooting Gerans Is Only One Mission
A second lesson from this photograph is the means the pilot used to dispatch the threat. Using the F-16’s gun preserves scarce air-to-air missiles. Ukrainian Air Force officials have acknowledged the pace of Russian air attacks imposes significant pressure on Ukraine’s missile inventories
Ukraine’s air force must perform several missions simultaneously: defend cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles; deter or engage Russian air forces; suppress enemy air defenses; conduct precision attacks into Russia; protect Ukrainian ground forces; and contribute to the broader intelligence and command-and-control picture. That requires both highly capable aircraft and scale.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in 2024 that Ukraine needed 120 to 130 F-16s to challenge the number of Russian aircraft committed to the war—many more than they currently possess. That was Ukraine’s stated requirement, not an independent assessment, but it illustrates the difference between possessing F-16s and operating a combat air force of meaningful size. Aircraft numbers by themselves, however, can also be misleading.
A force of 100 fighters is inherently smaller than it seems. At any given moment, some are undergoing maintenance while several must be earmarked for training. The aircraft left must be dispersed, protected, and repaired. Pilots must get enough flying hours to remain proficient. Weapons, engines, spare parts, and ground support equipment must be continuously available.
Airpower depends on a system—not simply an inventory of airplanes.
Building an Air Force, Not Donating Aircraft
One of the more consequential developments in Western assistance to Ukraine is largely unseen, but vitally important. The Air Force Capability Coalition has gradually moved beyond simply transferring F-16s to Ukraine toward creating a Western-style aviation ecosystem encompassing combat aircraft, pilot and maintainer training, weapons, logistics, protected infrastructure, command and control, and airborne early warning.
Ukraine’s future force architecture also includes French-built Mirage 2000s and Swedish Gripens alongside U.S.-made F-16s.
This is the correct way to think about airpower: A modern fighter becomes dramatically more effective when it is properly supported. Airborne early-warning aircraft that can see hundreds of miles, ground-based sensors, secure datalinks for sharing targeting info, and commanders able to assemble those inputs into a common operational picture all enhance operational performance.
There are legitimate questions about cost, training capacity, sustainment, competing aircraft types, and the rate at which any fighter force can realistically be expanded. Discussion about offering newer F-16s miss the point that doing so would not eliminate the need for ground-based air defense, inexpensive drone interceptors, or other cost-effective ways of defeating mass attacks. No country can economically afford to use its most sophisticated weapon against every inexpensive threat.
But the strategic distinction is important. The F-16s flying over Ukraine today began as an emergency wartime capability. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry now describes the broader effort as a transition from its Soviet aviation inheritance toward a modern, networked Western model. That transition will ultimately be far more consequential than any individual aircraft transfer.
The image released this week captures the beginning of that story: A pilot in the Ukrainian Air Force maneuvering an F-16 over Ukraine while the wreckage of a Russian cruise missile falls toward the earth. The next chapter is about whether Ukraine’s wartime collection of fighters evolves into the sustainable, technologically modern, and fully integrated air force it needs, with the capacity to defend its airspace for decades—and carry the fight to the aggressor if required.
That is the difference between providing Ukraine airplanes and helping Ukraine build a credible air force.

articles.title: European intelligence chiefs warn Russia could test NATO within months
articles.body:
European intelligence officials are warning that Russia could seek to test NATO in the coming months, potentially through a limited incursion into alliance territory, drone attacks or other provocations, as concerns grow that Moscow is preparing to escalate its operations in Europe.
One European intelligence chief told The Guardian that such an attack could come within “months, not years,” although other senior officials cautioned that there are no indications an attack is imminent and warned against fueling public panic.
The warnings, published Sunday, came after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that intelligence assessments indicated Russia could seek to test the military alliance in the coming months. French President Emmanuel Macron described the Polish warnings as well-founded and documented and on Friday summoned political party leaders and candidates in France’s 2027 presidential election for emergency talks in Paris on the issue.
Concerns about escalation are mounting as world leaders gather in New York this week for the annual UN General Assembly and as Russia and Ukraine intensify aerial attacks in the war that began with Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones and missiles at Moscow and other parts of Russia early Sunday in one of its largest aerial operations since the war began. Russia said about 1,600 drones were involved in the attack, including hundreds targeting the Moscow region.
In separate interviews with The Guardian, three senior European intelligence officials described the assessments behind the warnings about Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service, or BIS, said that in addition to a large-scale drone attack, a limited Russian incursion into NATO territory bordering Russia could be among the scenarios being considered.
“It's possible,” Koudelka said in a rare interview with the British newspaper. He said possible Russian actions could include “a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” adding that many people were working to prevent such a scenario. Koudelka said an escalation could happen in “months, not years.”
Officials in the Baltic states offered more cautious assessments, warning that amplifying speculation about a Russian attack on NATO territory could itself serve Russian President Vladimir Putin’s objectives.
Normunds Mežviets, director general of Latvia’s State Security Service, said his agency had seen no evidence of an imminent Russian attack.
“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” he said, while adding that there were indications Moscow was preparing for “more decisive” action in Europe.
Mežviets said it remained unclear whether such preparations were part of a broader strategy to destabilize Europe as the war in Ukraine approaches its fifth year. But he welcomed what he described as a change in attitudes among Western European governments toward the threat posed by Russia.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mežviets said, Baltic governments repeatedly warned their Western European partners about Moscow but were often ignored. That changed after the invasion, he said, when Western officials acknowledged that the Baltic states and Poland had been right about the threat.
‘Social media panic’
Estonian Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov also pushed back against what he called “panic on social media” over the possibility that Russia could attack NATO territory to test the alliance.
If there is reason to fear an attack, the Estonian government will say so, Vseviov wrote on X, urging the public in the meantime to remain calm and carry on with their daily lives.
The senior intelligence officials interviewed by The Guardian declined to describe the specific intelligence underlying their assessments.
They also declined to say whether CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow last month was intended in part to warn the Kremlin against attempting to test NATO.
Thomas Nilsson, head of Sweden’s Military Intelligence and Security Service, also spoke with the British newspaper and expressed skepticism about Moscow’s willingness to negotiate seriously over Ukraine.
Nilsson said he had seen no indication that Moscow genuinely wanted negotiations, adding that his assessment was that Russian leaders still believed they could achieve their strategic objectives and were therefore engaging in what he described as “negotiation theater.”
Nilsson, Koudelka and Mežviets agreed that Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other covert operations in Europe was likely to intensify and expand in the coming months.
Nilsson described an incident in which an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany as a “gamechanger.” German authorities have blamed Russia for the August incident, saying evidence indicated the Russian state provided expertise and equipment to operatives recruited to carry out the attack. Moscow has denied involvement.
The drone, carrying explosives, was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate, but German authorities said the device could have caused a catastrophe.
Sending an armed drone into a busy airport in the heart of Europe represented a significant escalation because it could have killed people or severely damaged critical infrastructure, Nilsson said.
He said Russia’s intensified sabotage campaign appeared to have several objectives: weakening European support for Ukraine, creating divisions within NATO and spreading fear across Europe.
Mežviets said Russia appeared to be shifting from relatively indiscriminate acts of sabotage and arson intended primarily to create panic toward attacks on specific targets linked to Western support for Ukraine.
“We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure,” he said, adding that European intelligence agencies were now seeing a shift toward targets in the defense industry.
Such operations, he said, could achieve both practical and psychological objectives, disrupting Western support for Ukraine while simultaneously spreading fear.
Koudelka said another consequence of the sabotage campaign was the strain it places on European intelligence services because even fires, accidents and technical failures with no connection to Russia increasingly require investigation as potential acts of sabotage.
Every fire or malfunction must now be examined by intelligence agencies as a possible terrorist attack, Koudelka said, describing that additional burden on security services as an outcome that benefits the Kremlin.
European governments have increasingly accused Russia of conducting what they describe as hybrid warfare across the continent, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this month that Russia had become “increasingly reckless,” citing incursions into NATO airspace, fires at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and the Leipzig incident.
Trump: ‘This ridiculous war must end’
Meanwhile, following one of Ukraine’s largest attacks on Russia since the start of the war, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday that the “ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended.”
Trump also said Russia had “unfortunately” lost control of parts of its diesel industry because of the war.
Ukraine launched about 1,600 drones toward regions across Russia overnight Saturday into Sunday, according to Russian accounts, with hundreds directed toward Moscow. The operation was among Ukraine’s largest attacks on Russian territory since the beginning of the war.
The assault came a day before results were announced from Russian parliamentary elections that produced an expected victory for Putin’s ruling United Russia party. Voting was also conducted in Russian-occupied regions of Ukraine, which Kyiv and the European Union denounced as illegal.
Reports from Moscow indicated that the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya, in the southeastern part of the capital, was hit. Videos circulating from the area showed smoke rising from several parts of the energy facility, which had also been targeted in June.
The refinery is a major supplier of fuel to Moscow and the surrounding region and is estimated to provide a significant share of the capital’s fuel needs.
The Ukrainian attack could add to tensions between Kyiv and Washington over strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump has expressed concern that such attacks could disrupt global fuel supplies and drive up energy prices.
Last week, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not to attack oil refineries deep inside Russia, arguing that the strikes were contributing to global fuel shortages and higher energy prices.
The following day, Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy facilities. Neither side confirmed such an agreement, and strikes on energy infrastructure have continued.
Zelenskyy did not commit to complying with Trump’s demand and responded with a statement disputing the U.S. president’s characterization of the situation.
Ukraine, Zelenskyy said, had proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia to stop attacks on critical infrastructure.
Food supplies, energy facilities and other basic infrastructure essential to civilian life should be protected, he said, accusing Russia of routinely attacking those targets.
Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics networks and even warehouses containing food and medicine continue to come under Russian attack, Zelenskyy said.
The intensifying strikes come as European security officials increasingly warn that the war’s effects are extending beyond Ukraine’s borders. While the intelligence chiefs interviewed by The Guardian differed over how imminent a direct Russian challenge to NATO might be, they agreed that Moscow’s covert and hybrid operations in Europe were likely to increase in the months ahead.

articles.title: ‘Bad idea’ or ‘betrayal’: Pentagon split pushed Trump to cancel Houthi strikes
articles.body:
President Donald Trump ordered the U.S. military to prepare for an attack in Yemen on Sunday at 5 p.m. local time. But three hours earlier — shortly after 2 p.m. — a new directive arrived: He had changed his mind, and the order was canceled.
NBC News reported overnight Monday into Tuesday on the dispute that preceded the cancellation and the dilemma facing the top ranks of the U.S. military over whether to intervene in the conflict between Saudi Arabia, a key American ally in the Middle East, and Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
According to two U.S. officials, senior military leaders were divided over whether Trump should intervene in the fighting, which has continued for several weeks amid Houthi advances and repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia, as well as on U.S. targets in the region.
The Saudis have appealed to Trump several times to act against the Houthis — a request that became more urgent in recent days after the rebels claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and advanced rapidly toward Marib province, home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.
According to the officials who spoke with NBC, some senior military figures have argued — both in Pentagon discussions and in conversations with Trump administration officials — that opening another military front in the region would be a “bad idea,” citing concerns that U.S. munitions stockpiles could be depleted.
Those officials also argue that the Houthis, at least for now, are not attacking American ships.
Other military officials, however, support some form of offensive action against the Houthis, arguing that Washington should assist Riyadh, particularly after the downing of the F-15, which poses a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen.
Those officials said senior figures who support that approach have privately voiced concern that a failure by the United States to take more decisive action against the Houthis would amount to nothing less than a betrayal of an important regional ally.
Trump had not planned to attack the Houthis or intervene, at least not until last Thursday. According to officials, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with him again that day and urged the president in phone calls to intervene, saying that “the kingdom cannot succeed on its own.”
According to one official, after that conversation Trump ordered the military to present him with new options for strikes against the Houthis.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine convened an emergency meeting in “The Tank” — the Pentagon’s most secure conference room — to discuss military options.
To do so, he canceled a trip to Copenhagen, where he had been scheduled to meet with NATO chiefs of defense who are simultaneously concerned about Russian escalation and possible Kremlin provocations on alliance territory.
‘Things Hezbollah took 20 years to develop, the Houthis developed in 5’
The New York Times reported Monday that Trump had already made the decision to intervene, and munitions had been loaded onto fighter jets that were ready for takeoff. But he then reversed course again and announced a change in plans.
The decision to cancel the strike — or at least delay it — stemmed in part from concern in Washington that opening another front could further complicate the parallel campaign against Iran, which has also stalled for now.
One senior U.S. military official in the region explicitly warned that action against the Houthis could pose serious risks to U.S. forces in the Middle East and to the mission connected to Iran, which includes imposing a U.S. naval blockade and conducting security operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
However, officials said the same senior figure also made clear that U.S. forces are capable of carrying out both the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis while reducing some of the risks involved.
Trump is expected to address the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering Tuesday. Just two days ago, responding to a question from Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst, he said he was “open to the possibility” of meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the gathering in New York this week.
He immediately added: “I’m in the process of making decisions. Very big things are going to happen. Iran had better behave.”
The internal rift within the U.S. military underscores the difficult position in which the president repeatedly finds himself, as the United States remains locked in a war with Iran — a war Trump himself initiated but has struggled to end — while also facing shortages of critical weapons and munitions.
Britain, however, may be able to help the Saudis, at least in part.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday night that he had agreed to a request from Riyadh to provide aerial refueling services for defensive purposes for a limited period. He described the move as one that “helps stabilize the wider region.”
“We received a request for military support from Saudi Arabia, and following the recommendation of the defense secretary and the foreign secretary, I agreed to the request to provide aerial refueling for defensive purposes,” he told reporters while traveling to New York to attend the UN General Assembly.
Britain and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, and Britain is among the kingdom’s largest arms suppliers.
Earlier this year, Britain deployed its Sky Sabre air defense system to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against Iranian missile attacks during the U.S.-Israeli war against the regime in Tehran.

articles.title: North Korea tests missile with maneuvering glide warhead
articles.body:
- North Korea fired two ballistic missiles from Wonsan on Sunday, with the second flying more than 600 km (370 miles), South Korea's military said.
- North Korean state media called it a test of a "new type of weapon," which analysts said appeared to involve a hypersonic glide vehicle warhead.
North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area toward the sea on Sunday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, with the second missile flying more than 600 km (370 miles).
Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch, and North Korean state media called it a test of a “new type of weapon.”
South Korea said the first missile launched around 3 p.m. local time and flew about 450 km (280 miles). The second launched roughly three hours later, at 5:50 p.m., and flew farther and higher, reaching an altitude of about 70 km (43 miles) compared with roughly 60 km (37 miles) for the first, according to flight data broadcast on North Korean state television and cited by open-source analysts. South Korean and U.S. authorities said they were still analyzing the missiles’ exact specifications.
North Korea’s Missile Administration said the test marked “a significant step in the technological development of its weapons systems,” and Kim said the advance would give an adversary “an incurable headache.” A monitor shown in North Korean state media footage was labeled “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory,” identifying the missile by name; North Korea did not publicly confirm what kind of warhead it carried. NK News, a Seoul-based outlet that tracks North Korea, said the projectile appeared to be an upgraded missile fitted with a hypersonic glide vehicle, a maneuverable warhead that separates from its booster and glides toward its target rather than following a fixed ballistic arc.
State media footage showed a flight-path graphic on a command-center screen that tracked the second missile through what appeared to be a pull-up maneuver, a sharp change in trajectory during flight that missile defenses have a harder time predicting. South Korean expert Chang Young-keun, cited by the Korea Herald, said the system paired a KN-23-style missile body with a hypersonic glide vehicle terminal section built to penetrate missile defenses while striking targets hundreds of kilometers away. He said it looked like a refinement of a system North Korea first tested last October rather than an entirely new weapon.
North Korea has tested hypersonic glide vehicles since September 2021, when it first flew the wedge-shaped warhead later associated with the Hwasong-8 missile. It has since tested at least two other missile types carrying similar warheads, the Hwasong-12B and the solid-fueled Hwasong-16B. In a January 2025 test of the Hwasong-16B, Japan estimated the missile flew about 1,100 km (680 miles) with an apogee near 100 km (62 miles); North Korea claimed a longer range and two separate apogees, an initial climb followed by a lower secondary peak consistent with a glide phase.
Sunday’s launches were North Korea’s 15th and 16th ballistic missile launches of the year, spread across nine test events, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said. That is roughly triple last year’s total of at least five missiles across four events, he said, calling the regional security situation “increasingly severe.” Japan lodged a formal protest, and South Korea’s National Security Council condemned the launch and called on North Korea to halt missile activity, saying it violated United Nations Security Council resolutions. The launches came about a week after North Korea’s previous test, on Sept. 12, and days after Pyongyang rejected a UN resolution demanding it halt its nuclear program.

articles.title: How Washington left Saudi Arabia’s plea for help unanswered
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Trump failed to answer Saudi plea for help against Houthis when Riyadh needed it most
Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.
But when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen's Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away.
For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.
The issue came to a head on Thursday when Mohammed bin Salman called Trump and urged him to intervene against the rapidly advancing Iran-backed group, according to the New York Times.
Trump had told advisers a day earlier that he opposed strikes. After the call, however, he changed course and ordered the Pentagon to prepare for an attack.
By Sunday, US commanders had reportedly approved target lists and troops were loading bombs onto warplanes. Then Trump reversed course again, calling off the strikes, at least for now.
So why did Trump stop short when one of Washington's closest Middle Eastern partners was asking for help?
Why is Saudi Arabia asking for US help?
Riyadh's plea comes at one of its most vulnerable moments in years, as the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi cities, oil infrastructure and shipping while making significant advances in western Yemen, taking the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coast including the area around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The threat has been compounded by the wider war with Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and increased Saudi Arabia's reliance on alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, a crucial route for bypassing Hormuz, has also been largely shut following an attack Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
That has left the kingdom facing pressure on its oil export routes from multiple directions.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh had spent decades investing in its US security partnership precisely for such a crisis.
"The reason a country like Saudi Arabia invests so heavily in developing a security partnership with the United States is for just this sort of eventuality," Ratney told the NYT.
Saudi officials have also made clear that they do not want to confront the Houthis alone after the kingdom's previous military campaign in Yemen became a costly, years-long conflict.
Why did Trump hesitate?
For Trump, intervening would mean opening another front while the US is already at war with Iran.
Most of his inner circle were either deeply sceptical of or opposed to joining Saudi Arabia's fight, amid concerns over pressure on the US military and its weapons stockpiles.
There were also doubts that another bombing campaign would work. The US struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets during a campaign lasting more than 50 days in 2025, but the group survived and has since rebuilt much of its military capability.
Trump has also stressed that the Houthis are currently targeting Saudi Arabia rather than the United States.
He said on Sunday that Washington had remained in communication with the group and that the Houthis had so far agreed not to fight the US. Houthi officials have disputed Trump's claim that they contacted Washington.
That gives Trump little incentive to restart a direct confrontation that could bring American ships back into the Houthis' sights and further threaten shipping through Bab al-Mandeb.
What does this mean for the US-Saudi relationship?
The Trump administration last week asked Congress to approve the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal estimated at $24.3 billion, saying it would strengthen the security of a "major non-NATO ally", can be an indication that Washington has not abandoned Riyadh altogether.
But advanced weapons sales are different from direct US military intervention, and the latest crisis has exposed the limits of what Riyadh can expect from Washington when their immediate interests diverge.
Saudi Arabia has already been looking to broaden its security partnerships. Last month, it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkey and Pakistan, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on all.
Turkey has since said it is prepared to help meet Saudi military needs as Houthi attacks intensify.
For Riyadh, it is a reminder that even close ties with Washington offer no guarantee of US support when American interests lie elsewhere.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy in US for UN summit

Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy in US for UN summit
Overnight missile and drone attacks hit several Ukrainian regions as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly.
Russian forces have launched widespread attacks targeting industrial sites and critical energy infrastructure across several regions of Ukraine, killing at least three people and knocking out power to nearly 100,000 residents, Ukrainian officials said.
The strikes overnight hit industrial facilities simultaneously in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dnipro, Pavlohrad and Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, regional Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram on Tuesday.

Three people were killed and six others were wounded in Dnipro, where missiles, drones and artillery heavily damaged business and warehouse premises, Hanzha said.
Ukraine’s air force said Moscow’s overnight barrage involved 212 drones, four cruise missiles, and an unspecified number of Oniks antiship and ballistic missiles.
The strikes also damaged energy infrastructure. An attack on a power facility left nearly 100,000 consumers without electricity in the northern region of Chernihiv, while in the Poltava region, Governor Vitalii Diakivnych said a “massive” Russian attack hit an industrial enterprise and a critical infrastructure facility.
The Russian Ministry of Defence confirmed its forces carried out major strikes, stating it hit industrial and military facilities, the fuel and energy sector, port infrastructure and sea vessels operating for the Ukrainian military.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Samara region along the Volga River, killing one person and injuring four, according to the local governor. The region hosts critically important facilities, including oil refineries.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence units intercepted and destroyed 297 Ukrainian drones across various regions overnight.
Diplomatic push in New York
The attacks come as Zelenskyy arrived in New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where talks on ending the war are set to be high on the agenda as nearly 130 heads of state gather.
The Ukrainian president wrote on X that a “drone deal” was ready to be signed to bolster air defence and secure funding for the war effort.
“Of course, Ukraine’s number one priority is bringing peace closer and protecting the lives of our people,” Zelenskyy posted. “There are concrete security proposals and de-escalation measures that could bring the end of the war closer. We are working to strengthen air defence and ensure sufficient financing for Ukraine.”
He said, “Around 20 meetings are planned, including with the US president, European leaders, US senators and members of the House of Representatives, heads of international organisations, leading American companies and think tanks.”
Zelenskyy met French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday and is likely to meet US President Donald Trump on Tuesday.
Earlier, Macron also met Trump, after which he said the two countries agreed to work together to secure a moratorium on strikes targeting energy networks and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine. Both Zelenskyy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov are set to address the UNGA later this week.

articles.title: Saudis may seek help from Israel as current alliances prove insufficient against Houthis - analysis
articles.body:
The sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has raised concerns that the confrontation could spread further across the region, with Washington worried that the conflict could intensify and potentially lead the Houthis to resume direct attacks on Israel, diplomatic officials told Maariv on Tuesday.
The officials said the key question is whether the situation can be brought under control or whether the confrontation will continue to escalate. Among the regional consequences being considered is the possibility that the Houthis could again try to attack Israel directly, as they did last year.
The concerns come after the US State Department updated its security guidance for American citizens in the Middle East, warning that the military confrontation between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia could escalate rapidly. The US Embassy in Israel also issued an alert urging citizens to remain vigilant and consider the possibility of flight disruptions, airspace closures, and transportation disruptions.
Diplomatic officials stressed that the updated and expanded warnings should not necessarily be seen as a sign that immediate developments are expected. The wording, they said, also reflects the administration's responsibility to warn American citizens in the region and make clear the seriousness of the situation should the confrontation intensify.
The warnings come against the backdrop of the latest escalation in the confrontation. Saudi Arabia confirmed that the Houthis launched a ballistic missile toward Riyadh, which was intercepted by the Saudi air defense system.
It was the first time the Saudi capital had been targeted since the current wave of escalation began. Residents reported hearing an explosion, and smoke was later seen near Riyadh's airport. No casualties or damage were reported.
The Houthis claimed they attacked "sensitive targets" in Riyadh with missiles and drones, as well as facilities belonging to oil giant Aramco in Yanbu. Saudi Arabia said it had also thwarted attempts to strike civilian infrastructure in Yanbu, Taif, Baish, and the Farasan Islands. Houthi claims that Aramco facilities were hit have not been verified.
Saudis divide efforts between defending territory, Red Sea shipping
The wave of attacks has forced Saudi Arabia to divide its efforts between defending cities and infrastructure from missiles and drones, securing energy facilities, and protecting shipping routes in the Red Sea.
In recent months, the Houthis have expanded their attacks on Saudi Arabia and shipping in the region, and in July they declared a naval blockade against the kingdom. Any disruption to traffic through the Bab al-Mandab Strait could significantly increase the economic and strategic cost of the confrontation.
Amid the tensions, US President Donald Trump returned to the White House from Camp David earlier than planned. No official explanation was given for the schedule change, and no confirmation links his early return to developments in the Middle East.
The return came as discussions were underway in Washington over the desired extent of US involvement in the confrontation. US media reported that options for action against the Houthis were examined while Trump was at Camp David, but no US decision to launch a strike was announced.
Washington has so far refrained from direct military intervention alongside Saudi Arabia in the current round of fighting and has not agreed to Riyadh's request to take military action against the Houthis.
Israel is closely monitoring developments. Israeli officials believe the pressure facing Saudi Arabia could also affect Riyadh's diplomatic calculations.
"Such an escalation could actually help the Abraham Accords," the officials said.
Israeli officials: Saudis recognizing alliances insufficient for Houthi threat
According to the officials, the Saudis are under pressure and are discovering that the relationships and alliances they have built are not currently providing a complete response to the threat. If the Houthi threat intensifies and the assistance the kingdom receives from its allies remains limited, they assess that Israeli capabilities could carry greater weight in the eyes of the Saudi leadership.
Saudi Arabia has been working in recent weeks to secure outside assistance. According to reports, amid a shortage of interceptors, it has requested air-defense assistance from France, the UK, Pakistan, and Egypt.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also traveled to Cairo and, according to the reports, sought Egyptian support against the Houthis.
Security cooperation among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is also being tested by developments on the ground.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Ankara was prepared to assist with Saudi military needs under the defense agreement among the three countries. Pakistan has so far not joined military action against the Houthis.
The gap between Riyadh's security needs and the assistance it is actually receiving is at the heart of the Israeli assessment. Israeli officials point in this context to the experience and capabilities Israel has accumulated in intelligence and air defense against the Houthis.
As the campaign continues, they assess that those capabilities could also become part of Saudi Arabia's broader considerations.
