articles.title: Putin's United Russia secures record Duma supermajority
articles.body:
President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party secured a record supermajority in the State Duma, officials said Monday, following a three-day election held without parties opposed to the Kremlin or Russia's war in Ukraine.
Electoral chief Ella Pamfilova said preliminary results showed United Russia – which has dominated Russian politics for 25 years – won 355 of the Duma's 450 seats.
The result handed Putin's party an increased supermajority and beat its previous record of 343 seats – giving it a free hand for constitutional changes.
The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.
The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions in Ukraine and hit ordinary lives in Russia more than ever this year.
Moscow has banned criticism of its military campaign and the only party that called for an end to the war – Yabloko – was barred for running for the federal parliament. It was, however, approved in some regions for local voting.
"These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a briefing with journalists.
Putin had encouraged Russians to vote in support of troops in Ukraine and Moscow also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
Pamfilova said turnout was over 59%, thanking Russians for voting despite what she called "psychological pressure on Russia."
Russia's Ukraine campaign broke its ties with the West. Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war Sunday, the last day of voting, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze.
"Despite the extreme situation, we were successful in ensuring the maximum security of these elections," Pamfilova told a Moscow press conference.
Forty-nine veterans who fought for Moscow in Ukraine are expected to enter parliament to represent United Russia, the party told Russian state media.
The Kremlin has sought to promote soldiers who fought in Ukraine into positions of authority when they return, with Moscow glorifying its troops.
While nobody in Russia doubted United Russia would win, the election did bring one unexpected result: in the Novgorod region, in western Russia, war-critical Yabloko entered the regional parliament.
On social media, Yabloko's Novgorod branch said it received some 12,000 votes – just over 6% of votes in the region – enough to enter the regional legislature.
"Peace, freedom and life without fear – these are the values that have struck a chord in people's hearts and souls," it said.
Russia's Communist Party came second in the vote, winning 40 Duma seats. The nationalist LDPR party took 25 seats and the New People party won 20.
The election result is expected to further tighten Putin's grip on power.
Some fear a new military mobilization in Russia. Putin has denied this while Kyiv accuses Moscow of planning a call-up in the coming weeks.
The election took place amid the escalation of the Ukraine war with no diplomatic solution in sight.
In some regions, voting also took place for the local heads.
In Chechnya, Ramzan Kadyrov – known for ruling the Muslim-majority republic – won 99.85% of the vote, the electoral commission said.
Opposing Kadyrov is hugely dangerous in Chechnya, which is known for extra-judicial killings.
Putin's political opponents are in exile, prison or dead – such as his main opponents Alexei Navalny who died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
The EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas dismissed Russia's "so-called" election.
"The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors. The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia," Kallas said.
In a joint statement, five countries including the U.K., Australia and Canada, condemned Russia's "sham" parliamentary elections in swathes of occupied Ukraine, branding the move "part of a wider system of occupation."

articles.title: Trump will pressure Zelenskyy in New York, demanding concessions regarding strikes on Russia – The Guardian
articles.body:
Trump will pressure Zelenskyy in New York, demanding concessions regarding strikes on Russia – The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
Trump plans to pressure Zelenskyy over a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure. Kyiv is ready to take steps if Russia stops the attacks.
U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to insist on an agreement on a mutual halt to Ukrainian and Russian strikes against energy infrastructure during his meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York. The Guardian reports, according to UNN.
Details
The presidents’ meeting is scheduled to take place on Tuesday on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly. The publication links Trump’s position, in particular, to the sharp rise in global diesel prices.
Ukraine has recently stepped up long-range strikes against Russia’s energy infrastructure. Last weekend, Ukrainian forces carried out a large-scale attack on the Moscow region, during which a major oil refinery in Moscow was hit.
Trump calls for strikes on Russian oil refineries to stop
On Monday, Trump said that Ukraine’s strikes had knocked out a significant portion of Russia’s diesel production capacity. At the same time, the U.S. president called on Kyiv to stop such attacks because of a fuel shortage on the global market.
According to The Guardian, during his visit to Ireland last week, Trump also urged Zelenskyy not to attack Russian diesel production facilities. On Sunday, the presidents held a phone call during which, according to the Financial Times, the issue of diesel fuel was one of the main topics.
The average price of diesel fuel in the United States reached a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, compared with $3.19 a year earlier. Prices rose amid the war with Iran, shipping restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz, and a reduction in Russian refining capacity.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready for reciprocal de-escalation measures if Russia stopped strikes against Ukrainian energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and facilities connected with food exports.
Last week, Trump said that an agreement on an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia had allegedly been reached. However, as The Guardian notes, the agreement was not actually finalized, and Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure continued.

articles.title: Trump and Iran Exchange Threats as Leaders Converge for Key U.N. Gathering. Can the Meeting Cool Rising Tensions?
articles.body:
Delegations from the U.S. and Iran are traveling to New York for the world’s largest diplomatic gathering this week in what experts say could be a key moment for determining the direction of the Iran war nearly seven months in.
Tensions between the warring countries are mounting ahead of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), with Iranian leaders and President Donald Trump exchanging a fresh round of threats.
Trump on Sunday weighed whether he should “blow the entire nation up” in an interview with Fox News, warning that Iran “better behave” and saying that “very big things” would happen in the war, without offering more detail. According to the outlet, Trump described his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”
A spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the U.S. were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons and capabilities,” according to Iran's Fars news agency. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi said.
The threats come after active hostilities in the conflict resumed in the last month when the U.S. and Iran traded fresh strikes amid tensions over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway in the global oil market. Meaningful negotiations between the two countries have meanwhile been stalled for weeks following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding leaders signed in June. And Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have further shaken the Gulf region by launching attacks against Saudi Arabia and capturing Perim Island, a strategic foothold in the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, another vital maritime trade route in the region.
Experts tell TIME that the U.N. General Assembly gathering, where delegations from Iran, the U.S., and key Gulf states will be in attendance, could offer a critical chance to deescalate the situation and attempt to revive peace efforts—although making progress in negotiations could be an uphill battle.
“This week in New York, there is an opportunity, especially for the mediating countries, to try to prevent tensions from once again spiraling, and potentially this time spiraling out of control,” says Ali Vaez, the deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group. “It's the last best opportunity to try to prevent an escalation either in October or in November.”
What to expect at this week’s U.N. General Assembly
Top officials from the U.S. and Iran will be present at the U.N. meeting this week, including Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and U.S. ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be in attendance as part of a slimmed-down delegation from the country. Both Trump and Pezeshkian are set to deliver addresses to the assembly.
Vaez says, however, that any effort to revive peace talks between the two countries during the event will largely rely on mediation by Gulf states.
Trump is set to hold talks with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council—a regional alliance including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain—on the sidelines of the gathering in the coming days. Sources with knowledge of the anticipated meeting told Axios, which first reported the news, that discussions are expected to concern next steps in the war with Iran, with a focus on U.S. ideas for a strategy after the conflict concludes.
Vaez believes that the Qataris could play a leading role in mediation efforts, with the support of countries such as Saudi Arabia, Oman, Turkey, Pakistan, and Egypt.
“It all depends on whether the mediating countries would be able to find a mutually acceptable formula,” he says of the possibility of the U.S. and Iran coming to some kind of agreement. “Because at this moment, both sides are in a zero-sum situation in which there is literally no overlap between what the Iranians demand and what the U.S. is seeking to achieve.”
Given what he characterized as maximalist demands from both the U.S. and Iran, Vaez contends that “some sort of a sweetener,” or incentive, must be given to each side for a deal to be reached, which he says may come in the form of revisions to the now-expired memorandum of understanding.
Sanam Valki, director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the policy institute Chatham House, agrees that it is far more likely that Gulf states mediate between Iran and the U.S. But, she adds, a direct exchange between U.S. and Iranian delegations is also a possibility—albeit a very slim one.
“The big question out there is: Will there be some sort of surprise encounter between the Iranians and the U.S.?” Valki says.
Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst on Sunday that he would be willing to meet with Pezeshkian during the U.N. gathering.
Beyond either mediated or direct discussions during the event, another potential outcome of this week’s General Assembly meeting is a United Nations Security Council Resolution regarding the Iran conflict, Vaez says. Unlike a memorandum of understanding like the one the U.S. and Iran previously reached, a security resolution would be legally binding by international law and would compel both parties to abide by certain conditions in the war.
Adopting a resolution would require the votes of at least nine out of the 15 members of the security council. And as a complicating factor, the U.S.—as well as the other four permanent members—would have the ability to defeat any such measure by casting a veto.
How could the U.N. meeting impact the Iran war moving forward?
“This is a very important week at UNGA for regional states, as well as the Iranians themselves, to try and roll back or manage how things evolve,” Valki tells TIME. “The President is very clearly weighing and considering the military options that are on his desk, which include not just responding to the Houthis, but another round of serious and severe strikes against the Islamic Republic.”
If a direct exchange between the U.S. and Iranian delegations does unexpectedly occur during the gathering, she says, “it's a big deal. It's a big outcome. It means that the Iranian president is willing to risk his standing at home, attacks at home, in order to stave off a serious military attack and build a direct lifeline to the Trump team.”
Up until now, both sides have sought “maximalist outcomes with minimal concessions,” Valki says. But Iran, through direct conversation with the U.S. delegation, could “signal a more transformational type of policy outreach, rather than the defensive reaction of traditional hardliners in the country.”
On Trump’s end, Vaez says the President could potentially make concessions to Iran by removing naval blockades on Iranian ports, rolling back sanctions against Tehran, or returning access to certain frozen assets. “That's what the President can put on the table … The most important thing for Iranians is economic reprieve and that's precisely where President Trump has tremendous leverage.”
A security council resolution, meanwhile, “could provide a degree of assurance about the sustainability of a new understanding between Iran and the U.S.,” Vaez says. He adds that through such a resolution, the U.N. could also establish an “observer mission”—what he describes as “an established mechanism that could look into disputes and adjudicate” if there are disagreements over alleged violations of the resolution, as there were previously over June’s memorandum of understanding.
Vaez stresses, though, that the odds of this week’s gathering resulting in a meaningful breakthrough in the stalled negotiations appears unlikely.
“There are very serious differences, and there's deep mistrust,” he says. “And so that's why I'm not very optimistic.”

articles.title: Rostec supplies latest Zubr anti-drone systems to military
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Rostec’s High Precision Systems Holding Company has delivered the latest Zubr anti-drone systems to the Russian Defense Ministry, which are designed to counter small, low-flying targets, the state corporation reported.
"The High Precision Holding of the Rostec State Corporation, has supplied the Russian Defense Ministry with the latest Zubr air defense systems intended to protect important facilities from small, low-flying threats. They are capable of independently detecting and tracking unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and can also be integrated into a unified, layered anti-drone defense system," the state corporation stated.
Rostec said that the Zubr is a close-in air defense system operating in the lower airspace where a rapid response to the appearance of UAVs and loitering munitions is crucial.
"The Zubr can be used both independently or integrated into a unified anti-drone defense architecture to build a layered air defense system for facilities. The system also serves as the last line of defense for large facilities, forming a unified air defense perimeter with them, including alongside the Pantsir missile systems," the state corporation specified.
In addition, the system is easy to maintain in the field and can be deployed rapidly. This is particularly important for a system that must remain constantly combat-ready, including at remote and poorly equipped positions, Rostec noted.
"The system developed by High Precision Systems is equipped with everything necessary for round-the-clock detection of drones of any size and their automatic tracking. Once the Zubr locks onto an aerial target, it engulfs it in a dense barrage of fire. As a result, at the final line of defense, where the system comes into play, enemy drones have virtually no chance of survival. "Zubr’s effectiveness is confirmed by its combat deployment experience and the steadily growing number of real targets destroyed by the system," said Bekkhan Ozdoyev, industrial director of Rostec’s Armament Cluster and board member of the Union of Russian Machine-Building Enterprises.

articles.body:
Mehmet Nuri Ucar and Serdar Dincel

An explosion rocked a crowded public market Wednesday in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz province, local sources reported.
The public market in the DhuBab area of Taiz, near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, was targeted by a ballistic missile, the sources said.
Panic broke out in the area following the attack, they added, but no information was immediately available on any deaths or injuries.
Footage shared on social media also showed a powerful explosion at the crowded public market.
The footage showed a large number of people around the market at the time of the explosion, followed by thick smoke and dust covering the area.
Media outlets close to the Yemeni government reported that the Houthis targeted the market with a missile.
Social media accounts close to the Houthis, meanwhile, also posted footage of the attack and claimed that it was an airstrike.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian oil refineries in Samara and Ufa
articles.body:
Ukraine hits Russian oil refineries in Samara and Ufa
Units from the Ukrainian defence forces struck two key oil refining facilities in Russia on the night of 21-22 September.
Sources: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine; Special Operations Forces (SOF)
Details: The Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara was struck.
The Special Operations Forces said the attack was carried out by Special Operations Forces' Deep Strike units jointly with the Unmanned Systems Forces and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine. Several drones reached their targets, causing a large-scale fire at the facility.
The Kuibyshev oil refinery is one of the largest oil refining facilities in Russia's Samara group and is part of the Rosneft structure. It has a refining capacity of around 7 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery produces petrol, diesel fuel, fuel oil and more than 30 other petroleum products.
The Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim oil refinery in Ufa, Republic of Bashkortostan, Russia, was also struck, with a fire reported on the premises.
Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim has a refining capacity of around 7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility carries out deep oil refining and produces petrol, diesel and boiler fuel, liquefied gases, sulphur and other petroleum products.
Products from both refineries are used to meet the needs of the Russian military.

articles.title: Diplomacy or war? Trump weighs next move on Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Diplomacy or war? Trump weighs next move on Iran
US President Donald Trump is weighing whether to pursue renewed diplomacy with Iran or further military action as he prepares for high-level talks with Gulf leaders in New York this week.
Trump is expected to meet representatives from all six Gulf Cooperation Council states - Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman - on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly's 81st session. The talks are expected to focus heavily on Iran and the future of the conflict.
The meeting comes as Qatar intensifies efforts to bring Washington and Tehran back to the negotiating table, with Qatari mediators exchanging proposals with both sides for nearly two weeks and shuttling between capitals in search of a breakthrough.
The diplomatic push is unfolding against an increasingly volatile regional backdrop.
Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, the group's advances around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have raised fears of further disruption to regional and global trade.
US embassies across the Middle East have also issued security alerts urging American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance amid the possibility of a rapid escalation, warning of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruption.
'An earthquake'
Qatar is trying to create a diplomatic opening before the conflict enters another phase.
Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani called for Gulf states and Iran to work towards a new regional security framework.
"Our region has experienced what I can only describe as an earthquake," Sheikh Mohammed said, arguing that Gulf states needed to work collectively to restore stability and improve relations with Iran.
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said on Sunday that Doha had spent nearly two weeks exchanging ideas with Washington and Tehran over the possibility of restarting negotiations.
"For around two weeks, we have been exchanging different ideas on resuming talks between Washington and Tehran," Qatari media reports cited Al Ansari as saying.
"We are working through our mediation team with Tehran and Washington to explore whether the talks can be resumed, and our mediators are currently travelling between different capitals in the hope of making progress on this track," he added.
"We have heard assurances from US administration officials that Washington wants to reach an agreement," Al Ansari said.
He also called for "a regional solution that brings stability and an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz", warning that "placing waterways under the sovereignty of a particular state and using it as a weapon would set a dangerous precedent for all of us".
The mediation effort could receive another opening in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are due to attend the UN General Assembly. Washington has agreed to allow a core Iranian delegation to attend despite the ongoing conflict.
Trump has also signalled that he would be open to meeting Pezeshkian during the gathering, although no such meeting has been announced.
'Blow the entire nation up'
The diplomatic manoeuvring comes as Trump publicly weighs whether to pursue negotiations or launch further military action against Iran.
Speaking to Fox News over the weekend, Trump said he was in "deciding mode" and warned that "very big things" would happen in the "not-so-distant future".
He described the options before him as destroying Iran, allowing the country to "rot" economically or reaching a deal.
"My question is, if and when, do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave," Trump said.
His comments followed similar remarks to Axios last week, when he said he faced a "big decision" over whether to resume large-scale attacks on Iran.
Trump had previously suggested the war could end after the November midterm elections, while accusing Tehran of seeking to influence the vote.
Iran, meanwhile, has warned that it was prepared for renewed large-scale fighting and would retaliate against another US attack.
Iranian media quoted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Hossein Mahdavi as saying Tehran would deploy new weapons and strike targets that had not previously come under attack if Washington launched another assault.

articles.title: Trump said that Russia had lost diesel capacity because of the war and called on it to end the war - Zelenskyy responded
articles.body:
Trump said that Russia had lost diesel capacity because of the war and called on it to end the war - Zelenskyy responded
Kyiv • UNN
Trump said that Russia's diesel industry had suffered losses because of the war and called on it to end the war. Zelenskyy reported on the dialogue and peace ideas.
US President Donald Trump commented on Russia’s loss of control over diesel production and stressed the need to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to his statement, emphasizing that dialogue with President Trump is ongoing and that ideas for bringing peace closer are on the table, UNN writes.
What Trump said
"Russia, unfortunately, has lost control of its diesel industry because of the war with Ukraine. A large number of their diesel refineries have been blown up and, at least temporarily, taken out of operation. This senseless and endless war with Ukraine must be ended. The entire world is suffering, while 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are killed every month. What a shame!" the US president wrote on Truth Social on September 21.
How Zelenskyy responded
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to a post by US President Donald Trump.
"Indeed, this Russian war against Ukraine and against common sense must be ended," Zelenskyy said on X.
The president noted that "from the first year of the full-scale invasion, its consequences have been far-reaching: the loss of many lives, the destruction of cities and villages, food security, energy problems, the extraordinary pace of technological development, including autonomous drones, and the rapid improvement of strike capabilities that had never existed before."
"Every new week of this war, let alone every new year, adds more and more problems. From the very first minute, Ukraine sought peace. We have already made dozens of diplomatic proposals on how to end this war with dignity, guarantee security, and prevent new Russian invasions," Zelenskyy said.
"Dialogue with President Trump and America is ongoing. There are also ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, beginning with decisive steps toward de-escalation. Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to corresponding de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible. We are ready to work on this, and we will discuss it with our partners on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. I thank everyone who is helping! It will no longer be the case that only the country that was attacked suffers. The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will also suffer. Technology makes this possible. The strength of countries’ leadership can—and must—ensure de-escalation, security, and peace. Thank you!" Zelenskyy emphasized.

articles.title: UN investigators warn Ukrainian, Russian attacks threaten civilians ahead of winter
articles.body:
Escalating attacks on infrastructure by Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, raising concerns about a repeat of last winter’s suffering.
The UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said on Monday both sides had intensified long-range strikes against civilian sites, including energy, industrial and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.
The commission said Russian attacks during the winter of 2025-2026 caused prolonged power and heating outages as temperatures fell to minus 20°C, leaving millions of civilians without adequate heating.
“Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries,” commission chair Erik Mose told the UN Human Rights Council.
The commission also voiced concern over reports of Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure inside Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, saying they indicated rising civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. It said it had been unable to investigate those reports because it lacked access.
“Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” Mose said.
The findings came after US President Donald Trump called last week for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, although neither side has confirmed it will participate.
Children, foreign recruits
The commission also reported on Russia’s imposition of what it described as patriotic education in occupied areas, including military training for Ukrainian children from the age of 14.
It said children were taught to handle weapons and carry out military drills.
Investigators also examined the recruitment of foreign nationals to fight for Russia, saying some had been deceived or coerced into joining the Russian armed forces.
Mose said agents and intermediaries had recruited people from various countries with promises of civilian jobs before they were allegedly compelled to sign contracts with Russia’s defence ministry.
Many recruits did not understand Russian or the contracts they signed and were subsequently sent to the front lines in Ukraine, he said.
The commission said some were killed, wounded, captured or went missing, leaving families searching for relatives from abroad.

articles.body:
Trump set for whirlwind UN meetings with wars in Iran, Ukraine on agenda
NEW YORK – US President Donald Trump is set for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with leaders from four continents at the UN General Assembly on Sept 22, against the backdrop of an unstable Middle East and a 4½-year-old war in Ukraine that shows no signs of abating despite the US President’s repeated attempts at mediation.
Trump is expected to start the day with a speech to assembled delegates, before meeting with no fewer than 11 world leaders, bilaterally or in group settings. While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump in 2025 caused a stir with a combative speech, saying that their countries were “going to hell” for, among other things, climate policy and mass migration.
Later in the day, Trump will meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy Rodriguez, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and the representatives of the Gulf states of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar.
In the evening, he may meet dozens more leaders, albeit briefly, during a leaders’ reception. Trump met with French President Emmanuel Macron on Sept 21. Additions to his Sept 22 schedule are possible.
The long list of foreign leader meetings reflects the US President’s focus on foreign affairs during his second term, during which he has started multiple wars, questioned longstanding alliances, threatened allies with invasion and sought to broker well over a dozen conflicts, with mixed success.
The US-Israeli war against Iran has been particularly consequential, driving up fuel prices globally, dragging down Trump’s approval ratings and presenting a challenge for Republicans running in the November congressional midterm election. On Sept 21, a Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Trump’s approval rating falling to an all-time low of 32 per cent, as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living.
Among the closely watched meetings will be the seven-way gathering with the Gulf leaders, many of whom are alarmed by the recent advances of the Houthis, Iran-backed militants who have captured wide swathes of Yemen, attacked US ally Saudi Arabia and threatened shipping through the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Political allies and opponents will also be closely watching Trump’s first-ever meeting with Venezuela’s Rodriguez, who rose to power with the Trump administration’s blessing after US forces snatched President Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York to face drug trafficking charges.
Trump’s allies say the US is working with Rodriguez to open Venezuela’s oil sector to US investment, but Democrats and some Republicans say his administration has not done enough to press for new elections in the South American nation.
During the meeting with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, its overseas territory, Trump will ink an accord designed to increase US military presence on the island while limiting that of geopolitical adversaries. Danish and Greenland officials hope the accord will put an end to Trump’s past comments suggesting he might take Greenland by force. REUTERS

Russia Could Use Properties in Sweden as Bases for Espionage and Sabotage
Russian-owned properties across Sweden could potentially be used as bases for espionage and sabotage, according to politicians and security experts, as the country still lacks legislation capable of preventing such property acquisitions.

According to SVT on September 21, properties with Russian owners are located across Sweden, and the Swedish Security Service (Säpo) has identified foreign-owned real estate as a potential security concern.
A survey conducted by the Swedish Defense Research Agency (FOI) identified 247 properties across the country owned by Russian actors.
However, the actual number could be considerably higher. FOI researchers had to manually examine around 10,000 names of property owners registered as living abroad. Properties belonging to foreign owners who reside in Sweden do not appear in the relevant registers at all.
Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson said intelligence-gathering activities in Sweden have increased, while Peter Hultqvist, the Social Democrats’ defense policy spokesperson, noted that the security concerns extend beyond properties located near military facilities.
“Russia is waging a hybrid war against Sweden and other countries. This could involve properties that could be used for sabotage in Sweden, espionage, or other efforts to undermine Swedish society,” Hultqvist said.
He also criticized the pace of Sweden’s response to the issue, saying that the previous years “have not been used optimally.”
According to SVT, Sweden has spent nine years examining the issue, yet no legislation has been introduced to prevent such property purchases.
Concerns over Russian-owned real estate have already surfaced in a case involving a property near the Muskö naval base in the Stockholm Archipelago. The Swedish Armed Forces have submitted a formal request to the government to take control of the 600-square-meter property, which is owned by the family of Russian businessman Stanislav Aleshchenko.

articles.title: Putin’s party wins supermajority in Russia’s parliamentary vote
articles.body:
Putin’s party wins supermajority in Russia’s parliamentary election
Victory of United Russia party strengthens Putin’s hand even as the war with Ukraine grows more unpopular.
President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party has won a record supermajority in tightly orchestrated parliamentary polls that excluded virtually any genuine opposition, near complete official results show.
With over 58 percent of votes secured, United Russia, which has dominated Russian politics for 25 years, is on track to win more than three quarters of the seats in the lower house, the State Duma, according to the results announced on Monday after three days of voting that ended on Sunday.
Recommended Stories

- list 1 of 4At least three killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow, says Russia
- list 2 of 4Is it a missile? Is it a drone? What’s the Pelican used by Ukraine?
- list 3 of 4Ruling party dominates early results in Russia’s wartime parliamentary vote
- list 4 of 4Russia election results show Putin’s party winning: What we know
The polls were the first parliamentary vote since Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022 and the first to include residents of four Ukrainian regions that were seized and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvedenko said the results, along with a high voter turnout of almost 60 percent, “is likely to be seen by Moscow as emboldening, as public support for what it is doing, especially for what it’s doing in Ukraine for the continuation of the war”.
Ella Pamfilova, chair of the Central Electoral Commission, said Yabloko, the only registered anti-war party in Russia, did not win any seats at the national level. It had been removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court and only had a few dozen candidates in single-seat races.
Yabloko did enter the regional parliament in western Russia’s Novgorod region. It said on social media that it received about 12,000 votes – just over six percent of votes and enough to enter the regional legislature.
Yabloko and the Communist Party, which has criticised some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of Putin, said many of their observers were turned away from polling stations.
The Communists made it into parliament with 13.8 percent of the vote, securing 40 Duma seats. The nationalist LDPR party won 25 seats and the New People party 20.
Russia did not invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which the Foreign Ministry has accused of “double standards” for its criticism of the country. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said the decision to exclude observers violated Russia’s commitments as a member.
‘Surprise to nobody’
Many Russians appeared unsurprised by the poll results.
“In the morning, I saw that United Russia was winning. It probably comes as a surprise to nobody,” said Moscow resident Tatyana.
Asked what she would like to change, she said: “Well, I guess everyone knows the most acute thing – the conflict in Ukraine. I’d like to see it end sooner, with peaceful methods if possible”.
The continuation of the war risks entrenching policies, which are increasingly affecting average Russians and the parliamentary supermajority may struggle to change the dynamic.
“Putin, of course, will interpret United Russia’s results as confirmation of the (public) support of the war, even though it is not the case: The overall demand for ending the war is growing,” said Tatyana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in an online commentary.
“The main question is: What now? There are great concerns about mobilisation, new repressions, harsher measures and escalation,” she wrote.
Western criticism
The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas dismissed Russia’s “so-called” election.
“The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine and shut out international election monitors. The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia,” Kallas said.
In a joint statement, five countries, including Australia, Britain and Canada, condemned Russia’s “sham” parliamentary elections in areas of occupied Ukraine, branding them “part of a wider system of occupation”.

articles.title: West using fake news against Global South – Lavrov
articles.body:
West using fake news against Global South – Lavrov
Fake news has become a routine Western tool for undermining competitors, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said. He argued that Western media have conditioned their audiences to believe negative reporting about countries portrayed as adversaries.
Russia’s top diplomat made the remarks during the opening ceremony of an international forum in Moscow dedicated to combating fake news.
RT has collected the highlights from Lavrov’s speech.
West abuses new technology to ‘derail multipolar world’
Modern information technology allows “any piece of news, even unverified or obviously fake, to be disseminated to millions, if not billions of people,” Lavrov warned. Western officials exploit this environment to “derail the creation of a just multipolar world order,” he added.
According to Lavrov, fake news is part of a broader set of tools the West uses against nations of the Global South.
Western efforts to obfuscate and distort the truth reflect a broader trend: its fear to compete honestly in virtually every sphere of human activity.
Unilateral economic sanctions, tariffs, and accusations of “industrial overcapacity” are being used against China, Lavrov said. Meanwhile, diplomatic pressure and blackmail in international organizations serve to obscure the fact that “on many key issues of modern development the West would have been left in absolute minority, should the voting be conducted fairly.”
Russia became a target after rejecting ‘neocolonialist cooperation’
Lavrov said Western pressure against Russia intensified in the early 2000s, when the country “began to liberate itself from neocolonial forms of cooperation with our Western colleagues.” That shift prompted the West to pursue a policy of containing Russia, he argued.
The minister cited several cases in which serious accusations were leveled against Moscow while, according to Lavrov, Russian requests for supporting evidence were rejected. He focused in particular on the so-called “Bucha massacre” – alleged mass killings of civilians near Kiev in 2022 that Moscow maintains were a Western-backed fabrication.
Lavrov criticized UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres for lending credence to the accusations and urged the public to examine a recent Russian investigation. He said researchers used publicly available Ukrainian sources, including obituaries and government databases, to trace people whose names Kiev placed on a memorial to alleged Russian victims in Bucha.
According to Lavrov, the list includes “dozens of names” of Ukrainian military personnel, members of the Security Service of Ukraine, territorial defense forces, police, and the national guard.
“Over 70 names have no digital footprint whatsoever, which is nearly impossible in today’s world,” Lavrov said, adding that “these facts disprove the claim that hundreds of civilians were killed in Bucha.”
West has ‘trained’ its citizens to swallow lies about Russia
Lavrov said Western media have for years deliberately “trained their public to trust any, even the most crazy anti-Russian tropes and fantasies.” Western governments take advantage of the rapid modern news cycle to make such messaging effective, he argued.
The essence of Western media policy: cook up some fake news, blow it up to the scale of a cosmic disaster for a day or three, and shut down access to any alternative views.
Lavrov cited a recent drone incident at an airport in Leipzig, Germany, which Berlin blamed on Russia while moving to close Russian diplomatic venues, as an example of that approach.
The West also simply ignores inconvenient facts, Lavrov said, pointing to Ukraine’s deadly drone attack on a vocational college dormitory in Starobelsk in May.
The incident killed dozens of students but “prompted no condemnation from Western governments and international organizations controlled by the West, and unfortunately barely made a ripple in the Western media,” he said.

articles.title: Pedro Sánchez announces the IA360 Plan and calls for a national agreement on the responsible, humane and safe deployment of artificial intelligence
articles.body:
Pedro Sánchez announces the IA360 Plan and calls for a national agreement on the responsible, humane and safe deployment of artificial intelligence
President's News - 2026.9.21
Moncloa Palace, Madrid
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during his speech at the event (Pool Moncloa/Sandra Armada)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has presented the IA360 Plan, which sets out a roadmap with specific actions to be implemented over the next 12 months to enable Spain to capitalise on the opportunities that artificial intelligence (AI) offers the economy, whilst prioritising public safety, trust and the protection of vulnerable people, particularly children. The plan will strengthen Spain's 'technological muscle', turn the adoption of AI into an 'economic driver and a breeding ground for talent', establish governance frameworks and promote a national consensus to provide security in the face of the changes to the labour market brought about by this technology.
This was announced by Pedro Sánchez during the closing ceremony of the 'IA360' event: 'Plan for the Responsible Deployment of AI', held at Moncloa Palace, and attended by the First Vice-President of the Government of Spain and Minister for Economy, Trade and Business, Carlos Cuerpo, who opened the event; the Second Vice-President of the Government of Spain and Minister for Labour and Social Economy, Yolanda Díaz; the Minister for Science, Innovation and Universities, Diana Morant; and the Minister for Digital Transformation and Civil Service, Óscar López. The event also featured a panel of experts, moderated by the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, María González, with contributions from the president of the AESIA (Spanish Agency for the Oversight of Artificial Intelligence) Think Tank, Senén Barro; Verónica Bolón, a lecturer in Computer Science and AI at the University of A Coruña; and Rosa Lillo, a mathematician and lecturer at Carlos III University.
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, during his speech at the event | Pool Moncloa/Sandra Armada
"We face a serious problem regarding how we are going to live and coexist" with AI, emphasised Pedro Sánchez, who pointed out that "if there is one thing that history shows, it is that self-regulation does not work and that the incentives of the few who control these cutting-edge industries will never be aligned with the public interest". He therefore called for "urgent action", warning that "unregulated, opaque AI, running amok and in the hands of a select few, is the perfect recipe for disaster". "If AI remains concentrated in the hands of a few companies and a handful of countries, its impact on shared prosperity - and on the very idea of democracy - will be devastating", he warned. He then went on to say: "Artificial intelligence without the guidance of collective human intelligence is not intelligence: it is chaos and stupidity".
However, he pointed out that, if we act "correctly", we will be able to "develop responsible, humanistic AI geared towards the collective good, which will enable us to build fairer societies", with "traceability and oversight", which will help to bridge social, geographical and economic divides, create new jobs, provide new tools for teachers and pupils, "democratise" access to new technologies and bring about improvements in productivity. "That future is not set in stone. Nor is it determined by the agents who are now striking fear into the hearts of their own creators. That future depends on us. "We will write it ourselves", he said.
Technological development: strategic projects and data centres
The President of the Government of Spain has unveiled the IA360 Plan to promote the responsible roll-out of Artificial Intelligence. The Action Plan, which sets out a roadmap with specific actions to be carried out over the next 12 months, aims to capitalise on the opportunities that AI offers the economy, whilst placing "public safety, trust and the protection of the most vulnerable, starting with children" at the centre. As he explained, the plan is based on four main objectives, which include strengthening Spain's 'technological muscle' through strategic projects such as the AI gigafactory and the development, in collaboration with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, of new AI models for use in tackling the climate emergency, energy and healthcare. It is also committed to developing data centres that "meet the highest energy and environmental standards and guarantee our sovereignty over the data stored there".
Artificial Intelligence Voucher and adaptation in Secondary Education and Vocational Training
The second objective, as Sánchez has indicated, aims to "turn the rapid uptake of this technology by society in Spain into an economic driver and a breeding ground for talent", through initiatives such as the Artificial Intelligence Voucher, aimed at SMEs and the self-employed, with the aim that by 2030 more than half of our businesses will have integrated AI into their operations. To achieve this, he emphasised the need to invest in talent and training, and therefore announced that the Government will adapt the secondary school and vocational training curricula so that students "learn to use and live alongside AI, but also to ensure that the roll-out of AI does not hinder their learning process".
AI governance: security will be a priority
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, closes the presentation of the IA360 Plan | Pool Moncloa/Sandra Armada
Another of the plan's objectives is to establish a framework for AI governance to tackle these challenges. In light of the "risks posed by uncontrolled AI" - which are becoming increasingly "apparent" in the light of statements made by some of its key players - Pedro Sánchez made it clear that "security will be an absolute priority in this Plan". This objective will be tackled on two fronts: strengthening the cybersecurity shield; and stepping up monitoring of the most aggressive frontier models. Finally, he stated that the plan will also promote "a genuine Social Contract on Artificial Intelligence - a national pact between businesses, workers, trade unions, parties and public authorities - to provide people with security in the face of the changes to work and life brought about by this technology". "Next month we will bring together the social partners to start making progress on this major national agreement", he announced.
Spain is starting from a "strong position"
In any case, Pedro Sánchez emphasised that Spain is in a "strong position" in the field of AI, as almost half of Spain's working-age population already uses generative AI, placing Spain sixth in the world in this ranking, second in terms of graduates from higher vocational training in ICTs, and with one in five companies already using AI on a regular basis. He added that "Spain has robust digital infrastructure, computing capacity and competitive renewable energy", adding that "Spain has understood from the outset that innovation and rights are not two divergent paths; that we can develop cutting-edge technology whilst, at the same time, demanding that it be secure, transparent and respectful of people".
Spain ranks second in the world for AI governance according to Stanford University; it was the first European country to set up an Artificial Intelligence Supervisory Agency and is spearheading the United Nations laboratory in Valencia. In addition, Pedro Sánchez pointed out that, under the Spanish Presidency of the EU, an agreement was reached on the European AI Act, the world's first comprehensive legislation of its kind. "Few countries have been as clear in their defence of humanist-inspired AI as Spain has been, and time is proving us right", he said.
Stepping up efforts on multilateral mechanisms: a 'bold' global agenda
The president emphasised that Spain has talent, businesses and a "dynamic" start-up ecosystem, connectivity and renewable energy; it is building the necessary infrastructure and, "above all, we have the moral authority as a country to drive a bold agenda at a global level so that we are not at the mercy of the monopolistic and abusive practices of the big tech companies". He specified that this agenda would "hold companies legally and financially accountable for the damage caused by their AI: 'deepfakes', mental health issues amongst our children and young people, or the theft of intellectual and industrial property". In this regard, he stated that Spain will "redouble its efforts", working with other countries, to ensure that AI at the frontier serves humanity, through multilateral bodies such as the European AI Office, the UN Scientific Panel, or the Global Dialogue, in which "Spain is a leading player, inspiring and guiding others through its commitment and vision".
"Some business leaders continue to argue that regulation is the enemy of innovation. They are wary of state power because they believe themselves to be above it. And they believe that, if there were to be any regulation, it is they who should lay it down. They couldn't be more wrong. It would be good if today's tech oligarchs did not fall into the same trap as the tycoons of the past, because "no one is above the public interest" and "nowhere is it written that technological progress guarantees social progress", he concluded, calling for the development of AI in Spain that "puts people at the heart of everything".
Carlos Cuerpo calls for "genuine access" and for confidence to be bolstered through "rules"
The First Vice-President and Minister for Economy, Trade and Business, Carlos Cuerpo, during his speech at the event | Pool Moncloa/Sandra Armada
The First Vice-President of the Government of Spain and Minister for Economy, Trade and Business, Carlos Cuerpo, stated that AI is "a technology capable of transforming the economy, classrooms, public services and our very lives", which will also shape the future of generations to come. In this regard, he pointed out that Plan360 will tackle the challenges arising from AI to ensure that this technology enables workers to "do things they could not do before" through incentives, address the high entry costs to prevent market concentration, and ensure genuine access for SMEs, the self-employed and in classrooms.
He also called for independent development, with our own companies, centres and models that form a "Spanish and European ecosystem on a sufficient scale to compete", as well as for the rules to be monitored and improved. The Vice-president called for efforts to draw up a "national plan" on AI developed "in partnership with society", and to this end announced that a round-table discussion will be organised involving experts, trade unions, businesses, scientists, academia, civil society and the public administration. Finally, he emphasised the importance of trust, with "rules, supervision, a roadmap and when one feels ready", so that "no one has to choose between blind enthusiasm and fear".

articles.title: 6 killed, 8 wounded in Saudi airstrikes on Yemen's port city Mocha: Houthi media
articles.body:
SANAA, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Saudi airstrikes hit a residential house in Yemen's strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in southwestern Taiz province early Tuesday, killing six people and wounding eight others, Houthi-run media reported.
According to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel, "Saudi aggression warplanes" carried out three airstrikes on a civilian residence in Mocha on Tuesday, killing six people, including two children and a woman, and wounding eight others.
Al-Masirah also aired footage showing children it said were among those killed and wounded in the strikes.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on the Houthi report.
The strikes came amid an escalating confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with Saudi airstrikes targeting Houthi-held areas across Yemen and the group launching missiles and drones at targets deep into the kingdom.
Mocha has become a major flashpoint in the renewed fighting. Houthi forces seized the port city on Sept. 10 before advancing south through Dhubab and taking Mayyun Island in the heart of the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Sept. 11, forcing Yemen's government forces to pull back toward defensive positions farther south.
Fighting has since intensified across the rugged highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandab, where government forces are battling to halt further Houthi advances and regain strategic positions along the vital shipping artery linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Beijing calls US sanctions on Iranian airlines illegal
articles.body:
China on Tuesday said it opposed "illegal" US sanctions on Iranian airlines, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened potential measures in a televised interview.
Bessent told CNBC that "all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world" in a matter of days under the weight of American sanctions, as the Trump administration seeks to ramp up pressure on Tehran.
Beijing slammed the threats on Tuesday, calling such measures "illegal".
"China consistently opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that lack a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun said.
The criticism comes on the eve of a summit between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
The United States and Iran have been at war since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic Republic's supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a broad offensive.
Tehran countered by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for energy transit, causing global oil prices to surge as the conflict spread in the Middle East.
The United States imposed sanctions this month on "all remaining Iranian airlines" that had yet to face such penalties.
The US Treasury Department also took aim at targets for supporting Iran's aviation sector, including firms based outside Iran.
"If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," Bessent said in the interview.
He had previously vowed the United States would declare "economic D-Day" on Iran and pledged to choke off Tehran financially.
Bessent's comments came a day after he met with Vice Premier He Lifeng for economic talks, laying the groundwork for the meeting between the two countries' leaders this week. (AFP) 
Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Lithuania prepares enhanced protection from drones for substation near Russia's Kaliningrad
articles.body:
Lithuania prepares enhanced protection from drones for substation near Russia's Kaliningrad
Lithuania plans to strengthen the protection of the new Gizai power grid substation near Kaliningrad Oblast, a Russian exclave, in particular by equipping it with special structures designed to protect transformers from drone attacks.
Source: European Pravda, citing Reuters
Details: Litgrid CEO Andrius Šemeškevičius stated that the substation is planned to be protected by a fence capable of withstanding the impact of a lorry laden with explosives, systems to detect possible underground tunnels and special reinforced-concrete structures to protect transformers from drone strikes.
"Previously, when designing our grid, we planned for natural disasters. Now, we think about all possible hybrid and non-hybrid threats," he said.
According to Šemeškevičius, the substation will occupy a 35-hectare site, so even a single drone strike would only damage a limited amount of equipment. He noted that the distance of the buildings from the fence provides protection "in case someone throws a Molotov cocktail inside".
Quote: "We are designing Gizai for a new reality... we are protecting ourselves from multiple Shahed drones, which could crash-land with 100 kilograms of explosives."
According to informed officials, the Lithuanian armed forces are advising Litgrid on the physical protection of critical energy infrastructure and countering modern threats.
The Gizai substation is planned to be built approximately 30 km west of Kaliningrad Oblast. It will become the first new facility in the region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Exclusive: Iraq PM to ask Trump for more time to disarm militias
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi PM to ask Trump for more time to disarm militias
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is expected to ask US President Donald Trump for more time to disarm pro-Iran militias when the two meet next week, an Iraqi government source told The New Arab.
The meeting comes as a 30 September deadline set by Baghdad to bring weapons held by militias under state control approaches.
The source said al-Zaidi intends to provide fresh assurances over his government's commitment to the disarmament process and ensuring that the Iraqi state retains a monopoly over the use of force.
However, he is also expected to raise the challenges facing the process and argue that more time is needed to implement it.
"Al-Zaidi will ask the US president not to impose financial or economic sanctions on Iraq," the source said.
They added that parties within Iraq's ruling Coordination Framework coalition were "pressuring al-Zaidi on this issue and are attempting to secure additional time for the process".
The source said resolving the issue by the end of September was no longer possible.
Al-Zaidi is scheduled to meet Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week.
The Iraqi government now appears to be seeking to manage the deadline rather than conclude the disarmament process by 30 September, potentially giving armed factions opposed to surrendering their weapons more time to reassess their positions.
"The committee established by the government to oversee the process of bringing weapons under state control is continuing its work, and pressure is building to turn the deadline from an endpoint into the starting point of a longer process," the source added.
Al-Zaidi had committed to Trump during a visit to Washington in July to resolve the issue of militia weapons by 30 September.
However, the government has struggled to make progress, with major armed factions refusing to surrender their weapons and allied political groups in parliament backing their position.
Iraqi armed groups have fired missiles at US-linked sites in Iraq amid the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran.
Washington has shown no sign of easing its commitment to the 30 September deadline, raising fears that the US could resume strikes on militia sites in Iraq.

articles.title: Putin’s Predictable Victory, Russia’s Uncertain Future
articles.body:
Putin’s Predictable Victory, Russia’s Uncertain Future
Russia’s elections were a staged affair, designed to legitimise Putin’s war on Ukraine. But elections have never decided Russia’s future. The latest ballots are no exception
Hardly anything in Putin’s Russia is more predictable than election results. During September’s three days of voting, Russians headed to the polls to elect deputies to the State Duma and regional officials. Yet, unlike in previous years, these elections took place at a time when Russians are feeling growing economic pressure and an increased sense of insecurity, driven by the success of Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes. These attacks have not only raised the costs of the war for Moscow but have also significantly strained a key Kremlin narrative, that after four and a half years of war, the regime is still able to insulate ordinary Russians from the direct impact of the conflict.
Possibly the biggest proof of this was Ukraine’s large-scale drone attack on Moscow on Sunday, 20 September, the final day of voting, bringing the war visibly into the capital. Rather than changing an already well-known election result, Ukraine exposed the widening gap between the Kremlin’s promise of security and the reality of a conflict that is increasingly reaching ordinary citizens at home.
Why Elections Still Matter?
Against this backdrop, the elections serve as an important instrument for showcasing legitimacy by demonstrating that Russians once again vote for United Russia, the party of government, thereby expressing trust in Putin and, by default, unquestioning support for his war effort in Ukraine.
To meet these goals, high voter turnout remains essential, but it must be carefully calibrated and tightly managed to avoid appearing excessive. Putin certainly has the tools to completely abandon elections, yet he prefers to present himself not as a dictator pursuing his own imperial ambitions, but as a strong, popular leader whose decisions reflect the will of the people.
Despite the predictability of the Duma elections, Russia faces an increasingly uncertain future
In a widely anticipated outcome, Russia’s ruling United Russia party secured a decisive victory in the country’s first wartime parliamentary election, winning approximately 58% of the party-list vote for half of the 450 State Duma seats, according to preliminary results released by the Central Election Commission. The party’s candidates also led in 208 of the 225 single-mandate constituencies, putting United Russia on track to retain its constitutional supermajority. This comfortable victory would allow Putin to claim that there is no internal pressure for the continuation of the war.
Campaign Messages
Throughout the campaign, two key themes dominated: national unity and the victory in the war in Ukraine, which go hand in hand, as well as social and economic reassurance. The messaging ahead of the vote demonstrated the central importance Putin attaches to the war. In an address on 16 September, he stressed every citizen’s responsibility to vote and to demonstrate unity around ‘common values, historical memory and love for the motherland’ He presented electoral participation as a demonstration that millions of Russians stand behind those fighting in Ukraine.
Victory in Ukraine and the rejection of compromise in any eventual negotiations were central to United Russia’s campaign rhetoric. Moreover, for the first time since 2007, the ruling party openly rebranded itself as Putin’s party. This is a shift from previous campaigns, because Putin is neither a formal member of United Russia nor a candidate on its list, and has generally tried to preserve some distance from official affiliation, even though it is widely understood to be his political tool. The return to personalised messaging, including the slogan ‘Being for Putin is the bare minimum,’ was intended to turn a vote for United Russia into a direct expression of support for Putin, his leadership and, most importantly, his conduct of the war.
At the same time, given the mounting economic grievances, regional campaigning mainly focused on familiar promises of improved public services, healthcare, wages and living conditions, while avoiding discussion of the war’s human and economic costs. This division of labour allowed the Kremlin to frame the national contest around patriotic rally around the flag while also offering voters, particularly in the regions, more traditional social and economic assurances.
Removing Symbolic Dissent
The dominance of the war as an electoral theme was also evident in the removal of even marginal sources of political opposition. By cancelling the registration of Russia’s only registered anti-war party, Yabloko, after it had initially been granted a right to run in elections, the regime demonstrated that there is no appetite to take even a very marginal risk. Yabloko had consistently polled in the low single digits, and even the call from Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, for anti-war voters to support the party was unlikely to have translated into a meaningful electoral challenge. The decision was therefore less about preventing Yabloko from winning seats than about closing the last formal political outlet for anti-war sentiment and maintaining complete control over the public narrative about the war in Ukraine.
Instead, the Kremlin elevated war veterans on United Russia’s candidate lists, presenting participation in the invasion as a route to political advancement and public recognition. This demonstrates that contribution to the war effort is rewarded, while also signalling to established elites that a new wartime political class is being based on demonstrated loyalty and service to Putin’s central political project.
Post-Election Uncertainty
Despite the predictability of the Duma elections, Russia faces an increasingly uncertain future. Putin may project satisfaction at United Russia’s landslide, but the vote does not resolve the problems he is currently facing. Ukraine is demonstrating growing confidence in its long-range strike campaign, increasingly targeting Russian cities and critical infrastructure. The Kremlin can manage public messaging, but it cannot blindfold citizens from the tangible consequences of the war when air-raid alerts, flight disruptions, fuel shortages and drone attacks become part of daily life.
Meanwhile, negotiations remain effectively stalled. Although Moscow may initially have judged the process to be moving in its favour, there is no indication that Ukraine or its partners are prepared to accept Russia’s maximalist demands, especially under the current status quo. Nor is Russia close to imposing those demands militarily. Its forces continue to make incremental territorial gains, but only at a slow pace and at a very high human and material cost. The prospect of capturing the entire Donbas region through battlefield advances or using limited gains to force Ukraine into accepting Moscow’s terms remains unfeasible.
Putin therefore faces a narrowing set of options, and one prospect that is causing growing concern among Russians is another wave of mobilisation. With the Duma elections now behind him, he may seek to present United Russia’s landslide as evidence of public backing for a more demanding phase of the war.
Several indicators suggest that the Kremlin may be preparing for this scenario. The National Guard has reportedly conducted mobilisation-related training and evacuation preparations, while its chief has issued a decree assigning the force responsibilities during a mobilisation period, under martial law and in wartime.
Although any new call-up would most likely be partial, it would still carry substantial political risks. The September 2022 mobilisation triggered a large outflow of Russians into neighbouring countries and generated considerable anxiety at home. A further and potentially more coercive wave could deepen war fatigue and undermine the Kremlin’s claim that it has successfully insulated ordinary Russians from the direct costs of the conflict.
It is unlikely that mobilisation alone would trigger regime change or mass nationwide protests. But, combined with Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia, deteriorating economic conditions and the cumulative exhaustion of a prolonged war, it could seriously erode the Kremlin’s ability to maintain the appearance of normality.

articles.title: FQ-42 Vengeance arrives for US Air Force tests
articles.body:
A new FQ-42 Vengeance Collaborative Combat Aircraft has been delivered to Creech Air Force Base in Nevada, where it will join US Air Force test and evaluation work on the service’s future uncrewed combat aircraft programme, according to General Atomics Aeronautical Systems.
The aircraft arrived at Creech on 18 September and will be used for further experimentation with the FQ-42, one of the designs being developed under the US Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft programme. GA-ASI was selected in April 2024 to build production-representative flight test aircraft, with the FQ-42 making its maiden flight in August 2025 before the company was selected for an initial production contract in June 2026.
Mike Atwood, GA-ASI Vice President of Advanced Programs, said: “The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible. Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”
The FQ-42 has already flown in formation with F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle aircraft as preparations continue for collaborative operations between crewed and uncrewed platforms. GA-ASI said its wider experimentation has also involved the XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and MQ-20 Avenger, with aircraft flown semi-autonomously and autonomously using different artificial intelligence pilots and under collaborative control from pilots flying F-22 Raptors and F-35s.
GA-ASI describes the FQ-42 as a low-observable uncrewed combat aircraft with an internal weapons bay and features intended to improve survivability. Further work will build on demonstrations previously carried out with the MQ-20 Avenger as a CCA surrogate, allowing collaborative control concepts to be tested alongside the main US Air Force development programme.
GA-ASI has completed a new low-observable paint facility for the programme and says it is positioned to deliver up to six aircraft a month to meet US Air Force requirements, with additional manufacturing space available if orders increase. The company is also using its own funding to continue FQ-42 production while government funding plans develop, and intends to build aircraft for its own fleet to support further testing and technology development.
The FQ-42 and XQ-67A are both derived from GA-ASI’s Gambit family of uncrewed combat aircraft, which uses a modular design intended to allow sensors, weapons and autonomy software to be integrated without major changes to the underlying airframe. The XQ-67A was developed with the Air Force Research Laboratory and has served as one of the flying predecessors to the FQ-42 programme.

articles.title: China and Europe should not fight trade wars: Wang Yi
articles.body:
China and Europe should not fight trade wars because the pair are comprehensive strategic partners, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his German counterpart in a call, according to a statement from Beijing.
Wang told German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul that strengthening mutually beneficial bilateral cooperation aligns with both sides' interests and represents the "right choice", the Foreign Ministry said late on Monday.
"China and the EU are comprehensive strategic partners; China and Europe should not fight trade wars," a statement from the ministry cited Wang as saying.
"China has consistently advocated that both sides move toward each other and find solutions to each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation," he added.
China hopes Germany maintains a rational and pragmatic approach and plays a positive role within the  EU, promoting the upholding of free trade and rejecting protectionism, Wang said.
Germany's foreign ministry said the two ministers agreed that a stable global economy is in China's, Germany's and Europe's interest.
"Trade relations have to be based on fair rules and a real level playing field," it said on social media platform X.
The two ministers also discussed Iran, Ukraine and the issue of Taiwan, the Chinese statement added.
China hopes Germany takes concrete action to maintain Chinese-German relations and peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, creating  necessary conditions for high-level exchanges, Wang said.
He noted that the one-China principle is the political foundation of China-Germany relations.
Wadephul responded by saying the German side firmly adheres to the one-China policy and the position will not change, Xinhua news agency reported.
Noting that the current international situation is facing a series of new threats and challenges, Wadephul said that Germany expects China to leverage its influence in international and regional affairs and work with Germany to explore solutions.
Germany supports the EU and China in properly addressing their differences through dialogue and is willing to play an active role in this regard, he added. (Xinhua/Reuters)
